title: Boehne explains why the Fed watches equity wealth when productivity accelerates
summary: Why should a central bank pay attention to rising equity prices when the profits behind them may reflect a genuine improvement in productivity? Philadelphia Fed President Edward Boehne's January 2000 answer was that share prices enter the outlook through household spending. Productivity gains can support higher wages and profits at the same time. Higher valuations, in turn, can lead shareholders to consume more and save less. The first development expands what the economy can produce. The second increases demand for that output. The net effect on inflation depends on which grows faster. Boehne gave no equity-price threshold for intervention and saw no case for targeting share prices themselves.

The figures available when he spoke made that distinction consequential. Since the end of 1995, real GDP had grown about 4¼% a year, real consumer spending more than 4%, and business equipment and software spending more than 13%. Payrolls had risen by about 2.5 million a year since 1991, and unemployment had fallen from above 7% to just over 4%. Yet inflation had declined in 1998 despite output growth above 4½%. Oil pushed headline inflation up in 1999, while core inflation showed no acceleration in Boehne's account. A forecast based on the historical relationship between low unemployment and higher inflation would have repeatedly called for price pressure that had yet to arrive.

Boehne distinguished temporary cost relief from changes he thought could last. The Asian slump had reduced commodity and import prices and sharpened price competition for US manufacturers in 1997 and 1998. Cheaper imports also boosted US purchasing power and contributed to the widening trade deficit. As foreign economies recovered and commodity prices turned back up, the continued stability of core inflation became harder to explain entirely by that earlier relief. He pointed to an average 2.7% annual rise in labour productivity since late 1995, nearly twice the pace of the preceding twenty years. Productivity continued to accelerate into the third quarter of 1999, unusually late in an expansion. This was his evidence for revising sustainable growth upwards, although it left open how far or for how long.

The speech gives an unusually concrete account of what higher productivity meant on firms' balance sheets. Computerised inventory control, communications and more reliable deliveries allowed a manufacturer to bring components to the line when needed. Fewer goods in storage meant less warehouse space, handling labour and short-term borrowing to finance the stock. An economy can therefore grow faster at the same time as part of companies' demand for working capital falls. Likewise, industrial capacity utilisation had fallen since 1995 despite rapid growth in aggregate demand. Firms had expanded the capabilities of existing facilities. Boehne also credited trade openness and deregulation with increasing competition, and budget surpluses with raising national saving available for investment. The speech does not estimate each factor's separate contribution.

Those supply changes posed a timing problem. Policy acts with a lag, so waiting for broad inflation to rise can mean reacting late. But persistently overpredicting inflation with an old relationship can induce an unnecessary tightening. Boehne expected some persistence of the productivity improvement and considered another year of strong growth, low unemployment and relatively low inflation plausible. The particular warning was about what happens when productivity ceases to accelerate. If demand, household wealth and wages have come to reflect ever-larger gains, even continued growth in productivity may leave less room for costs and consumption to rise at the same pace. The resulting risk is conditional on demand and unit costs. A slower increase in productivity alone is insufficient to infer the next rate move.

Boehne devoted the final part of the speech to how innovations reached production. Young service firms with few assets to pledge had limited access to conventional bank loans. Angels and venture funds could supply risk capital with an expected exit in roughly five years through acquisition or flotation. He cited more than $6 billion a year in new US venture-fund commitments in recent years, against less than $1 billion annually before 1979. A complementary network of development centres, incubators and repeat founders supplied management advice, shared facilities and experience. The number of US business incubators had risen from 12 in 1980 to about 600. These levels measure access to finance and support. They do not measure the productivity ultimately generated by the firms.

He underscored that distinction with survival evidence. Almost one fifth of the companies on a 1985 list of 500 fast-growing private companies had disappeared or failed by 1995. That selected cohort differs from the more than 160,000 US businesses started and over 80,000 failures he reported for 1997. Dividing failures by starts in the same year would therefore yield a misleading estimate of a new firm's failure probability. His more modest claim was that easier access to finance and expertise let more firms try an idea. Whether that produced durable macroeconomic gains depended on diffusion into existing firms as well as successful entrants.

questions.question: How could policymakers detect that demand had begun to outrun the new supply capacity before core inflation rose?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the output, hours, compensation, unit costs and profit margins available before each decision. Compare industries with fast capital deepening against industries with little new investment. If productivity remained strong while unit costs and margins were stable, tight labour markets alone would give a weak inflation signal. Productivity slowing across both groups while compensation remained firm would change that inference.

questions.question: Did rising equity wealth translate into consumption independently of the stronger future incomes households expected?
questions.detail: Link changes in household spending and saving to pre-existing equity exposure, income growth and the timing of market gains. Distinguish owners of liquid portfolios from households with pension wealth that is hard to spend. Compare estimated consumption responses with revisions to expected earnings. A rise in both spending and equity prices driven by the same income news would otherwise overstate a direct wealth effect.

questions.question: Did venture funding and better inventory management produce measurable gains beyond the expansion itself?
questions.detail: Follow cohorts of funded and comparable unfunded firms and their customers. Track output per worker, inventory-to-sales ratios, short-term borrowing and exit, allowing for failed firms as well as surviving issuers. Observe how established manufacturers adopting new systems perform when orders slow. The funding totals and incubator counts in the speech document wider access, but following production and financing through a downturn would test whether operating improvements persist.
